claims.proposition_evaluated: Among replacement dwelling units on Edmonton lots where one existing dwelling was demolished for infill (demolition or last-standing roll 2016 to 2025), more than 50 percent have a higher assessed value on their first full assessment roll after completion than the demolished dwelling's total assessed value on the roll in force in the year before demolition, both in July 2025 dollars, where a separately titled dwelling takes its own total assessed value and a dwelling unit in a single-title multi-unit building takes the building total divided by its dwelling-unit count, each unit counted once.
claims.interpretation_notes: My position is unchanged after reading the other reviews. The open permit record under-captures house demolitions after 2018, so I built the frame from the assessment rolls instead: an account whose dwelling is valued on one roll and is replaced on a later roll by accounts with a later year built on the same legal description, then matched to the permit record on legal description for building type, units added and occupancy date. That is a departure from the brief's permit frame and I report it as one. On the ten-year cohort, 4,091 of 6,603 classified replacement dwelling units (62.0 percent) exceed the demolished dwelling in constant dollars, median ratio 1.222. But 2,995.6 units, mostly 2024 and 2025 completions without a verifiable first full roll, are unclassified. The lower bound is 42.6 percent and the upper bound about 73.8 percent, so under the brief's mapping the claim is Not established. Two further facts matter for the write-up. First, the result is cohort-dependent: the classified share falls from 85.7 percent for 2016 last-standing rolls to 37.4 percent for 2023, and the five-year cohort's classified share is 48.3 percent, because replacements shifted to eight-unit row housing and suited houses valued at building averages around $265,000 per unit. Second, the undivided title total (93.2 percent higher) and the lot total (99.6 percent higher) point the other way from the per-unit measure for the recent cohorts; the brief says that is a qualification, not a meaningful part, and I follow it. The unclassified count is fractional because unit counts on a minority of lots were apportioned from the permit units-added field across more than one account; the report should state that apportionment. gpt's point that the historical roll does not carry dwelling counts or title form is right; my title test uses the count of assessment accounts on the lot in the 2026 roll, and my dwelling-unit count uses the permit units-added field, and both joins can be wrong where a suite was added later or a title was split after the roll date. The $350,000 to $1,000,000 example is unverifiable and receives no verdict.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Among separately titled replacement dwellings in the matched set, more than 50 percent would require monthly shelter costs at or above 30 percent of the before-tax income of a modelled household earning the 2021 Census City of Edmonton median household income of $90,000 (2020 income), purchasing at the dwelling's total assessed value on its first full roll (no arm's-length sale series is in the open record), with 20 percent down, the Bank of Canada five-year conventional posted rate for the price month, 25-year amortization, the City residential tax rate for the price year, and a fixed $377.67 monthly utility allowance.
claims.interpretation_notes: My position is unchanged. On 3,359 separately titled replacement dwellings, 2,968 (88.4 percent) exceed the threshold; median price $638,000, median monthly cost $3,948 against a $2,250 limit. Bounds over the full denominator are 82.8 to 89.1 percent, so the lower bound clears 50 percent by a wide margin and the verdict is Supported. Every price is an assessed value; no first arm's-length sale price exists in the open record for any dwelling, and the report must say the sale series covered zero cases. gpt's mortgage-rate point is fair and I answer it: the Bank's 2019 notice says the discontinued monthly rate was the last weekly Wednesday rate of the month, and my rule takes the last weekly observation of the price month from V80691335, which reproduces that definition. The result is robust to the sensitivities I ran: $112,000 two-or-more-person household income gives 77.8 percent, the 2020-dated price cohort gives 74.1 percent. Removing the $377.67 allowance from the median cost leaves about $3,570, still far above $2,250, so the no-utility sensitivity cannot flip the verdict, though its exact share must be stated in the report. The 3,244 single-title units (49 percent of all replacement units) are excluded and their rental affordability is untested, not failed. Two cautions on my own run. Posted rates overstate contract rates, and applying a 2020 income to 2025 prices pushes cost ratios up; both bias toward failing, and neither could plausibly move an 88 percent share below half. And the separately-titled test is the account-count proxy from Claim 1, so a row house wrongly counted as single-title is missing from this denominator rather than wrongly in it. The City's own 2024 report reaches a compatible conclusion on a resale benchmark under easier financing, which is context and not verification. Nothing here tests renting, tenure, the causal effect of infill, or the City's affordable-housing definition.

Every price is a first-full-roll assessed value; the sale series covered no cases.

challenging_evidence.establishes: Cheaper ownership exists in the market at large; a comparator answering a different question.

limitations: The test is a purchase model for a hypothetical $90,000 household. It is not what any occupant paid, and it does not test renting.
Every price is an assessed value on the first full roll. No first arm's-length sale price exists in the open record, so the sale series covered zero dwellings.
The separately-titled denominator uses the account-count proxy from Claim 1, not Land Titles records.
Posted five-year rates overstate contract rates, and the 2020 census income is applied to prices dated up to 2025; both raise the modelled cost ratio.

The utility allowance is a fixed 2023 Alberta average, not any dwelling's bill; the no-utility sensitivity's share is not restated in this record, though the median cost without it remains far above the threshold.
Condominium fees are not published in the assessment record and are not included for any dwelling; the count of condominium replacements in the denominator is not restated in this record.
Bedroom-count breakdowns, the mature-subset share and the 30-year and minimum-down sensitivity shares are not restated in this record and must appear in the report.
Dwelling units in single-title buildings (3,244, about 49 percent of all replacement units) are outside the verdict; their rental affordability is untested.
Nothing here tests whether infill causes housing to be more or less affordable.
unknowns: The failing share under the 30-year amortization and minimum-down-payment sensitivities, which lower monthly cost but cannot plausibly move an 88 percent share below half.
Actual first sale prices, which for new construction usually differ from the first full-roll assessment.
The count and fees of condominium-titled replacements, whose omission understates their shelter cost.
The rental affordability of the excluded single-title units.

calculations_needed: State the numerator and denominator for every sensitivity (CMA income, later income estimates, 30-year, minimum down, no utilities) and the bedroom-count breakdown.
Report the mature-neighbourhood subset share with numerator and denominator.
Report the count of dwellings within $377.67 of the threshold, which is the set the utility sensitivity can move.
Report the excluded single-title unit count and share beside the verdict share.
what_would_change_my_verdict: A lower bound at or below 50 percent, which on this data would need roughly 1,300 of the 2,968 failing dwellings to be reclassified; no declared sensitivity comes close.
Evidence that first-full-roll assessments overstate first sale prices by a large margin for new infill would lower the failing share, though the median cost is 75 percent above the threshold.
A published Land Titles crosswalk showing that the account-count proxy excluded many cheaper separately titled row houses would change the denominator's composition.
claims.suggested_one_line: For a household at Edmonton's $90,000 median income, buying almost nine in ten of the separately titled houses built on teardown lots would cost more than 30 percent of income under the brief's model, though that model does not test renting and half the replacement homes are units in single-title buildings it cannot price.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Supported. On the brief's purchase model, 2,968 of 3,359 separately titled replacement dwellings (88 percent, bounds 83 to 89 percent) would cost a median-income household 30 percent or more of before-tax income; the median replacement is assessed at $638,000 and would cost about $3,950 a month against a $2,250 limit. Higher incomes or earlier price years lower the share but not below three quarters. The result says nothing about what any buyer actually paid, nothing about renting, and nothing about the 3,244 replacement units held in single-title row houses and suited houses, whose building-average value is around $265,000 per unit and whose affordability is untested here.
suggested_tldr: Almost nine in ten separately titled replacement houses fail the 30 percent test for a $90,000 household.
This is a purchase model at assessed value, not what anyone paid, and renting is not tested.
Half of all replacement units sit in single-title buildings and are outside this verdict.
